title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Replace combinational division with an iterative EX divider
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz on the Tang Nano 20K. Its 199.837 ns
critical path crosses the forwarding mux, EX ALU, and arithmetic logic before
a memory-side register. The ALU currently contains four combinational / and
% expressions, which create a deep divide path even though DIV and REM are
infrequent compared with ordinary CoreMark instructions.

Use one shared, 32-bit restoring divider for DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU in EX,

title: Move division into an eight-cycle execute unit
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz, and its 156-cell worst path crosses
forwarding and the EX ALU before reaching the memory interface. The ALU
contains full-width combinational division and remainder, a likely source
of that depth and of the 12,312-LUT area. CoreMark spends far more cycles
on ordinary instructions than on divisions, so a bounded divide latency
should be repaid by a substantially shorter clock period.

title: Predict direct loop and jump targets in fetch
motivation:
The current fetch PC always advances by four until a branch or jump resolves
in EX. Each taken loop back edge therefore discards the younger fetch and
decode work. CoreMark executes many short loops, so avoiding those bubbles
can improve iterations per cycle even if the existing ALU path still sets
Fmax. No earlier predictor attempt appears in the bench experiment history.

title: Isolate critical execute paths from unrelated selection logic
motivation:
The iterative-divider champion reaches 49.199 MHz. Vendor timing shows two
nearly tied 25.3 ns paths: register-file data traverses EX branch resolution,
the fetch NOP mux, and load-use hazard logic before returning to the ID
register or PC enable; forwarded data also traverses the general ALU's DSP
multiplier selection before reaching the data-memory address. Both paths
contain selection logic unrelated to the result required at their endpoint.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Isolate the two timing endpoints from unrelated EX logic. Feed load-use
comparison with the raw instruction-memory rs fields and qualify it only
with imemReady, so branch redirect no longer passes through the fetch NOP
mux and then a register-address comparison to drive PC/ID controls. The
existing redirect priority makes any wrong-path load-use match harmless.
In EX, derive equality and signed/unsigned less-than branch predicates in
parallel and compute target alignment using only low address bits. Add a
dedicated rs1-plus-immediate effective-address register for LOAD/STORE and
drive the data-memory address from it, so the general ALU's multiplier and
result mux have no path to that memory port. Keep the general ALU result
for architectural writeback and retain the existing stalls, redirects,
misalignment traps, and RVFI values. Shortening both tied paths should
increase Fmax without changing CoreMark cycles or divider latency.

title: Move fetch squashing to the ID register boundary
motivation:
The current champion's worst timed path traverses EX branch resolution,
IF instruction masking, hazard control, and the ID/EX register. IF replaces
the entire instruction word with a NOP whenever a redirect or instruction
stall occurs. That puts a 32-bit control mux before decode and register-file
addressing, even though the downstream pipeline already carries validity.
This path limits Fmax at 49.199 MHz and costs every CoreMark instruction.

title: Predict recurring control transfers with a small target table
motivation:
The current core fetches sequentially until EX resolves each taken branch or
jump, discarding two younger instructions. A previous stateless predictor cut
CoreMark cycles by about 6%, but it was measured on the old combinational
divider design, whose 5 MHz arithmetic path dominated timing. The present
iterative-divider champion runs at 49.199 MHz and can benefit from fewer
branch bubbles only if prediction preserves its clock frequency.

iterative-divider champion runs at 49.199 MHz and can benefit from fewer

hypothesis.hypothesis:

counter. Predict a target only on a tag hit with a taken counter; otherwise
fetch PC+4. Train conditional branches from their resolved EX outcome and
train JAL as always taken. Leave JALR sequential because a shared return
instruction can have several call-site targets. Carry the predicted next PC
with each instruction and redirect in EX only when it differs from the
architecturally resolved next PC. The target table replaces the fetch-side
instruction predecode and target adder that the earlier predictor needed:
the common prediction path is a shallow tag lookup and mux. Gate training
on a legal, aligned EX instruction actually advancing, reset only entry
valid bits to allow compact table storage, preserve predictions across bus
stalls, and give a misprediction correction priority over fetch stalls.
This should remove most recurring loop and direct-call bubbles without
materially lengthening the current critical path.

title: Cut the two tied execute-to-register timing paths
motivation:
The current champion reaches 53.736 MHz. At the median placement option,
vendor timing shows two paths only 0.045 ns apart: a register-file read
traverses the unsigned multiplier DSP and ALU result mux into EX/MEM;
a forwarded branch operand traverses EX branch resolution and the IF
redirect back to a reset pin on an ID payload flop. Improving either
path alone would expose the other, so both need a local timing cut to
clear the champion's 4.6% acceptance margin.

title: Pipeline a shared multiplier outside the one-cycle EX ALU

multiplier DSP, and result selection before the EX/MEM register (24.595 ns,
13 cells). The EX ALU computes three full-width multiply variants alongside
ordinary arithmetic. Earlier divider unrolling showed that adding
arithmetic depth to EX harms Fmax, while the one-bit-per-cycle divider
demonstrated that a small latency cost can buy a much faster clock.

motivation:
The champion loses two younger instruction slots whenever a taken branch or
jump resolves in EX. A 32-entry tagged target buffer reduced CoreMark cycles
from 4.49 million to 4.22 million, but its extra storage and routing lowered
Fmax from 53.736 to 49.253 MHz and reduced fitness. Direct branch and JAL
targets are already encoded in the instruction, so storing full targets and
PC tags is unnecessary for the common control transfers.

title: Remove wide pipeline-register control mux chains
motivation:
The 140.56-fitness champion is limited by a 41-cell path from a register-file
read through EX branch resolution and IF redirect back to an ID/EX source-value
register. ID currently clears the entire wide pipeline bundle on redirect or

title: Split the EX bypass across the decode register
motivation:
The current 196.80-fitness core is limited by a 16.655 ns, 40-cell path

title: Buffer predicted-path instructions across pipeline stalls
motivation:
The existing fetch predictor already removes bubbles for many backward branches
and direct jumps, but fetch stops whenever decode, execute, or data memory
stalls. The independent instruction bus is often ready during those cycles.
With about 22% random instruction stalls, retaining instructions fetched in
those otherwise idle cycles can prevent later front-end bubbles. The prior
return-stack attempt saved only 0.58% of cycles and hurt Fmax, so buffering
the established direct-target prediction is the stronger predictor angle.

motivation:
The 213.82-fitness champion is limited by a 15.9 ns feedback path from
ID/EX's registered direct-EX bypass lane, through operand selection and

correction signal, which currently zeroes the entire EX input bundle.

bubble to break these loops would lose throughput.

title: Keep speculative fetches in a circular queue without redirecting its payload
motivation:

Retain the four-entry predicted-path prefetch queue, but implement it as

the reset occupancy discards it. Keep the empty-queue direct bypass so an

the existing aligned branch/JAL prediction for each accepted instruction.

prevent their delivery to decode. Separating queue validity control from
its wide data registers should remove the measured correction-to-FIFO-PC
path while retaining most of the observed 9% cycle reduction, enough to
exceed the 4.6% fitness threshold if Fmax recovers above about 90.6 MHz.
